title: PVC & PPR Pipes in Bali Villas: Why They Leak
meta: Why PVC and PPR pipes leak in Sanur villas—UV damage, joint failures, PDAM pressure—and how to plan a replacement without tearing up your floors.
intro: Most villa leaks in Sanur trace back to one of two pipe types: grey PVC or white PPR. Both are perfectly serviceable materials on paper, but tropical UV, salt-laden air, and PDAM pressure swings put them under stress that simply does not exist in a temperate-climate apartment block. The good news is that spotting early warning signs can save you from a flooded bathroom at 2 a.m. during the rainy season.

sections.h2: Which Pipes You'll Find in a Bali Villa
paragraphs: Walk into most pre-2015 villas along Jalan Raya Sanur or the smaller lanes off Jl. Bypass and you will find grey PVC running from the rooftop tank down through the walls to every tap, shower head, and toilet cistern. Builders chose it because it was cheap, easy to cut, and available at any hardware shop in Denpasar.

Newer builds (roughly 2016 onward) tend to mix systems: PPR for hot-water lines coming off the geyser or solar heater, and either PVC or PPR for cold water fed by PDAM mains or a bore well. Some projects use PPR throughout. What you end up with depends entirely on what the contractor had in stock that week.
bullets: Rooftop storage tanks (usually 1,000–3,000 L) sit above the main distribution point.
Cold-water runs typically drop vertically behind one wall before branching horizontally under floors or inside ceiling voids.
Hot-water loops are shorter and often run alongside the kitchen or bathroom wall.
Pool circulation pipes are a separate system—usually larger-diameter PVC—and should not be confused with domestic plumbing when diagnosing a leak.

paragraphs: PVC is a thermoplastic. In a cool climate it stays flexible for decades. In Bali's heat cycle—midday sun baking an exposed pipe to 50 °C+, then a cooler night—the material expands and contracts thousands of times a year. Over five to eight years the polymer chains lose elasticity and the pipe becomes brittle.

The most common failure points are the solvent-cement joints. The glue creates a chemical bond, but repeated thermal cycling and any slight vibration from PDAM pressure surges will eventually open a hairline gap at the socket. You may notice a slow weep that appears only when the tank is full and the house is pressurised.

Another frequent issue: kinks. If a builder routed a pipe around a structural column without a proper elbow, the plastic develops a permanent bend. That weakened spot is where cracks start, usually on the outer radius of the curve.

sections.h2: Sunlight, UV, and the Sanur Coastline
paragraphs: Sanur sits on the east coast with almost no tall buildings between you and the equatorial sun. Any PVC or PPR run that is visible on a terrace, balcony, or exterior wall gets direct UV exposure for ten-plus hours a day. UV breaks down the stabiliser additives in the plastic, turning it chalky white (PVC) or yellowed (PPR). A pipe that looks faded is already losing structural strength even if it has not cracked yet.

Add the salt-laden sea breeze and you get a second stressor: corrosion on any metal fittings—brass elbows, chrome tap connections, or the steel brackets holding pipes to walls. Corroded brackets can shift a joint just enough to break the seal over time.

During the rainy season (roughly November to March), persistent moisture accelerates both UV damage and biological growth inside poorly sealed joints. If your pipe runs are exposed, shade them or re-route them behind a wall as soon as practical.

sections.h2: When It's Time to Reroute Your Plumbing
paragraphs: A single small leak does not automatically mean you need to rip out every pipe. But there are clear signals that the whole run is past its useful life: the pipe surface feels soft or spongy when you press it; the colour has gone uniformly pale; you have had two or more separate leaks in the same section within a year; or the villa is older than ten years and still on original PVC.

PDAM pressure also matters. Sanur's supply can fluctuate noticeably between morning peak and late night. A pipe that barely survives 1 bar may fail at 3 bar during a surge. If you notice drips only at certain times of day, the pressure variation is likely the trigger rather than a one-off defect.

As a rule of thumb: if you are replacing one 2-metre section, inspect the entire run end-to-end. Adjacent sections installed at the same time with the same batch of material will be at the same stage of degradation.

sections.h2: Planning a Pipe Replacement Without Chaos
paragraphs: Start by mapping the affected run. Turn off the main valve (usually near the rooftop tank or at the PDAM meter), open the lowest tap to drain residual water, and photograph every joint before you cut anything. These photos help me quote accurately from WhatsApp without needing an extra site visit.

Coordinate timing. If your septic tank needs desludging or your pool filter pump is due for service, schedule those in the same window so you are not opening the same floor slab twice. The dry season (April–October) is ideal because any accidental splash dries quickly and there is less ambient humidity to complicate curing of new joints.

Protect finishes. In older Sanur villas the walls may be plaster over bamboo lath; cutting into them releases dust that settles everywhere. Lay drop cloths, seal off adjacent rooms, and agree on a realistic timeline—rerouting a full bathroom supply line typically takes one to two working days including pressure testing before the wall is closed up.

Before we backfill or re-plaster, I will pressurise the new run and hold it for at least thirty minutes while you check every connection. No paint, no tile grout, no ceiling board until that test passes.
bullets: Photograph all existing pipes and fittings before work starts.
Confirm whether the feed is PDAM mains, well water, or both—pressure ratings differ.
Agree on material: PPR for hot lines, PVC or PPR for cold, depending on routing and exposure.
Schedule septic, pool, or electrical touch-ups in the same visit to avoid repeated access.
Insist on a pressure test before any surface is restored.

faq.q: Can I just glue a cracked PVC pipe and keep using it?
faq.a: A solvent-cement repair on a clean, dry cut can buy you a few weeks, but it does not restore the original strength of the joint. If the surrounding pipe is already chalky or brittle, the next crack will appear nearby. Treat a glued patch as a stop-gap until you can schedule a proper section replacement.

faq.q: What is the practical difference between PVC and PPR in my villa?
faq.a: PVC (grey) handles cold water well and is easy to cut on site; it becomes brittle with UV and heat cycling. PPR (white or green) tolerates higher temperatures, making it the standard choice for geyser and solar-heater loops. Both last many years if kept out of direct sun, but PPR generally ages more gracefully in Bali's climate.

faq.q: Should I replace every pipe at once or only the leaking section?
faq.a: Replace the failing section plus any adjacent run that shows the same age and condition. A full whole-villa reroute makes sense when the system is over ten years old, has had multiple leaks, or you are renovating anyway—because you will be opening walls regardless. For an isolated weep in an otherwise sound system, a targeted swap is usually sufficient and far less disruptive.

cta: If you've spotted a weeping joint, a discoloured pipe behind your kitchen sink, or a crack running along the terrace wall, snap a clear photo and send it over WhatsApp—I'll tell you whether it needs a patch today or a full reroute this month.
